definition: A keystone is the central piece that everything else depends on — originally the wedge-shaped stone at the crown of an arch that locks all the others in place.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word keystone. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know keystone should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Ecologists call the sea otter the kelp forest's keystone: remove it, and the urchins mow the whole underwater forest down.
A component is much weaker than a keystone: one working part among many, swapped out with nothing worse than a repair bill — the whole barely notices.
A mainstay is strong but still weaker than a keystone: losing a mainstay hurts the whole badly, while losing the keystone is how you find out the whole was an arch.

the pin through an axle that keeps the wheel from sliding off — the small part a whole scheme quietly depends on. Keystone makes the same claim with an arch behind it: without a linchpin things work loose; without a keystone they come down.

the first stone laid, the one a building is squared and raised from — the founding element. A cornerstone is where something begins; a keystone, set last at the crown, is what holds up everything already standing.

When the county cut the late bus to save money, attendance at Jefferson High's after-school programs collapsed within a month — tutoring, robotics, and the jazz band all at once.
The bus, it turned out, was the keystone: every program stood only because students had a way to get home at six.
Keystone is the right word because nothing about the bus looked important — it was the humblest line in the budget — yet every other piece leaned on it.
Like the wedge at the crown of an arch, a keystone is proven not by how it looks but by what falls when it goes.

Keystone is a load-bearing word, not a spotlight: a centerpiece is what everyone looks at, while a keystone is what everything leans on — and plenty of keystones (a late bus, a quiet clause) go unnoticed until they're gone.
Distinguish it from cornerstone, the founding stone something is built up from: cornerstones start; keystones hold.
Ecology borrowed the word for keystone species — the otters and wolves whose removal collapses a whole web.

For sixty years, everything in Calder Flats ran through the rail junction: grain went out on it, machinery came in on it, and half the town drew a paycheck from it.
The hotels served its passengers, the elevator companies timed their season to its schedule, and the banks lent against its freight receipts.
Locals called the junction the keystone of the town's economy, and the rerouting of 1928 proved them right.
When the railroad moved its main line forty miles south, Calder Flats did not decline gradually.
The hotels closed within two years, the elevators within five, and the banks called in their loans.
A town built around one indispensable piece had learned what happens when that piece is pulled.
